## Measures can rank the same models differently

Most pages so far have scored models by the RMSE, with R² beside it now and then. Both are
**performance measures**: numbers that sum up how far a model's predictions fall from the
observed values. Each measure weighs the misses its own way, so two measures can rank the
same models differently, and a model can win on one by being wrong in a way the other
ignores. This page sets four measures side by side, shows why they part on skewed counts,
and shows which of them can see predictions that are too low across the board.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Four measures weigh misses differently

A **miss** is the observed value minus the prediction, at one station. The four measures
below turn a set of misses into one number.

| Measure | What it is | What it minds most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **RMSE** | the square root of the average squared miss | large misses |
| **MAE**, the mean absolute error | the average size of a miss | every unit of a miss the same |
| **Poisson deviance** | the average Poisson loss | a miss compared with the count predicted |
| **R²** | one minus the squared misses over the squared spread of the observed values around their average | the same misses as the RMSE, compared with predicting the average |

[Statistical modelling and machine learning](../01-introduction/what-is-machine-learning.qmd#the-test-error-is-a-typical-miss)
built the RMSE by hand. MAE and the Poisson deviance appeared in
[Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd) as losses, the quantities a
fit makes small. The same formula can serve as a loss during fitting and as a measure
afterwards, and the two need not match: a forest fitted with squared error can be scored by
MAE. For the first three measures, lower is better. R² is 1 for perfect predictions, 0 for
predictions no better than the average of the observed values, and below 0 for worse.

Each measure is smallest at a different prediction, as each loss is in
[Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#each-loss-aims-at-a-different-middle-of-the-data).
The RMSE and the Poisson deviance are smallest when a model predicts the **average** of
the values it could observe, and MAE when it predicts the **median**, the middle value.
For counts with a long right tail the median sits below the average, so MAE favours
models that predict low.

The **mean absolute percentage error** (MAPE), common in forecasting, divides each miss
by the observed value. A count of zero makes it undefined, and on the other counts it
punishes a prediction that is too high far more than one that is too low, so it does not
suit counts.

## R² has two definitions

The R² reported so far in this course is yardstick's `rsq()`, the **squared
correlation** between the observed and predicted values. The textbook R² in the table
above is `rsq_trad()` in yardstick and `r2_score()` in scikit-learn. For a linear
regression scored on the data it was fitted to, the two are equal. On new data, or for
any other model, they are not, because the squared correlation asks only whether the
predictions rise and fall with the observed values. Predictions that are all too low
by the same proportion keep a perfect correlation.

::: {.diagram}
![Two definitions of R². Left, predictions in the right pattern but too low: the squared correlation is perfect, and R² is low because it counts the gap to the line where the predicted value equals the observed one. Right, predictions at the right level with scatter: both measures agree. The two definitions rank the two sets of predictions in opposite orders.](img/two-r-squared.svg){fig-alt="Two cards, each a scatter of eight predicted values against observed values, with a dashed line where predicted equals observed. Left, right pattern, too low: the points lie on a straight line of half the slope, below the dashed line; squared correlation 1.00, R² 0.17. Right, right level, scattered: the points sit above and below the dashed line; squared correlation 0.73, R² 0.70. A note says squared correlation asks how closely the points follow some straight line, whatever its slope, and R² asks how close they come to the dashed line: one minus the squared misses, divided by the squared spread of the observed values around their average."}
:::

## Worked example

Four models predict the survey's counts:

- **Predicting the average**: every station gets the average count of the fitted
  stations. It has no skill, and the other three should beat it.
- **Poisson regression**, from
  [Count regression](../03-supervised-learning/count-regression.qmd), with each input
  entered as a straight line.
- **Random forest**, from
  [Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd).
- **Random forest on log counts**, the same forest fitted to the log of the count plus 1,
  each prediction turned back into animals, as in
  [Distributional assumptions](../06-assumptions-limitations/distributional-assumptions.qmd#training-on-log-counts-predicts-far-fewer-animals-than-were-caught).

Every model is cross-validated on the same ten folds of sites, and each measure is worked
out from the pooled out-of-fold predictions, as on
[Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd). Every measure therefore scores the same
predictions of the same stations.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() |>
  mutate(log_abundance = log1p(abundance))

set.seed(61)
folds <- group_vfold_cv(survey, group = site_id, v = 10)

inputs <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
            "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")

with_inputs <- function(outcome, model) {
  recipe(reformulate(inputs, outcome), data = survey) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    workflow(model)
}

forest <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 1) |>
  set_mode("regression")

average <- null_model(mode = "regression")
log_forest <- "Random forest on log counts"

models <- list(
  "Predicting the average" = with_inputs("abundance", average),
  "Poisson regression"     = with_inputs("abundance", poisson_reg()),
  "Random forest"          = with_inputs("abundance", forest),
  "Random forest on log counts" = with_inputs("log_abundance", forest)
)

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold <- map(models, \(model) {
  fit_resamples(model, folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)) |>
    collect_predictions() |>
    arrange(.row) |>
    pull(.pred)
})
# back from log counts to animals
out_of_fold[[log_forest]] <- expm1(out_of_fold[[log_forest]])

predictions <- as_tibble(out_of_fold) |>
  mutate(caught = survey$abundance) |>
  pivot_longer(-caught, names_to = "model", values_to = "predicted") |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model))

tibble(stations = nrow(survey),
       `average catch` = round(mean(survey$abundance), 2),
       `median catch` = median(survey$abundance),
       `stations with none` = mean(survey$abundance == 0))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, mean_poisson_deviance, r2_score,
                             root_mean_squared_error)
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
caught = survey["abundance"]

folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=61)

inputs = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu",
          "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
numeric = [c for c in inputs if c not in categorical]

def with_inputs(model):
    recipe = ColumnTransformer([
        # scaling leaves an unpenalised fit unchanged and helps the solver
        ("numeric", Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                              ("scale", StandardScaler())]), numeric),
        ("nominal", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
    ])
    return Pipeline([("recipe", recipe), ("model", model)])

# max_features="sqrt" draws a few inputs at each question, as ranger does.
forest = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, max_features="sqrt",
                               min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=1)

models = {
    "Predicting the average": DummyRegressor(),
    "Poisson regression": PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000),
    "Random forest": forest,
    # fitted to log counts, each prediction turned back into animals
    "Random forest on log counts": TransformedTargetRegressor(
        forest, func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1),
}

# every station's out-of-fold prediction from each model, in the survey's order
out_of_fold = {name: cross_val_predict(with_inputs(model), survey[inputs], caught,
                                       cv=folds, groups=survey["site_id"])
               for name, model in models.items()}

predictions = (pd.DataFrame(out_of_fold).assign(caught=caught)
               .melt(id_vars="caught", var_name="model", value_name="predicted"))

pd.DataFrame({"stations": [len(survey)],
              "average catch": [round(caught.mean(), 2)],
              "median catch": [caught.median()],
              "stations with none": [(caught == 0).mean()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
pct <- function(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 1)
```

The counts are skewed: the average station caught `r f2(mean(survey$abundance))` animals,
the median station `r median(survey$abundance)`, and `r pct(mean(survey$abundance == 0))`
of the stations caught none.

### RMSE and MAE choose different forests

The Poisson deviance has no yardstick function, so it is written out as in
[Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd#counts-and-presence-have-their-own-losses).
The last column adds up each model's predictions over all the stations and divides by the
number of animals caught: 1 means the model predicts the right total.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: measures
# a station with no catch adds only its prediction
poisson_deviance <- function(caught, predicted) {
  per_station <- ifelse(caught > 0, caught * log(caught / predicted), 0) -
    (caught - predicted)
  2 * mean(per_station)
}

scores <- predictions |>
  summarise(RMSE = rmse_vec(caught, predicted),
            MAE = mae_vec(caught, predicted),
            `Poisson deviance` = poisson_deviance(caught, predicted),
            `predicted / caught` = sum(predicted) / sum(caught),
            .by = model)

scores |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
scores = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False)
          .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
              "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(g.caught, g.predicted),
              "MAE": mean_absolute_error(g.caught, g.predicted),
              "Poisson deviance": mean_poisson_deviance(g.caught, g.predicted),
              "predicted / caught": g.predicted.sum() / g.caught.sum(),
          }), include_groups=False)
          .reset_index())

scores.round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: measure-numbers
#| include: false
score_of <- function(name, measure) scores[[measure]][scores$model == name]
best_on <- function(measure) as.character(scores$model[which.min(scores[[measure]])])
rmse_rank <- rank(scores$RMSE)[scores$model == log_forest]
```

The RMSE picks the **`r str_to_lower(best_on("RMSE"))`**, at
`r f2(score_of(best_on("RMSE"), "RMSE"))`, and the Poisson deviance agrees. MAE picks the
**`r str_to_lower(best_on("MAE"))`**, at `r f2(score_of(best_on("MAE"), "MAE"))`, a model
that comes `r c("first", "second", "third", "fourth")[rmse_rank]` of four on the RMSE,
behind Poisson regression.

The last column shows why. The forest on log counts predicts
`r pct(score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals caught; the other models
predict close to all of them. Fitted to log counts, it aims at the median catch, below the
average, and MAE rewards exactly that. For a stock estimate or a map total, MAE has picked
the model that misses `r pct(1 - score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals.

### The squared correlation cannot see the shortfall

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: r-squared
r_squared <- predictions |>
  summarise(`squared correlation` = rsq_vec(caught, predicted),
            `R²` = rsq_trad_vec(caught, predicted),
            .by = model)

r_squared |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
r_squared = (predictions.groupby("model", sort=False)
             .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({
                 # yardstick's rsq() is the squared correlation,
                 # and its rsq_trad() is r2_score()
                 "squared correlation": np.corrcoef(g.caught, g.predicted)[0, 1] ** 2,
                 "R²": r2_score(g.caught, g.predicted),
             }), include_groups=False)
             .reset_index())

r_squared.round(3)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: r-squared-numbers
#| include: false
r2_of <- function(name, measure) r_squared[[measure]][r_squared$model == name]
```

The forest on log counts has a squared correlation of
`r f3(r2_of(log_forest, "squared correlation"))`, about as high as the random forest's
`r f3(r2_of("Random forest", "squared correlation"))`: its predictions rise and fall with
the catch as well as any model's do. Its R² is `r f3(r2_of(log_forest, "R²"))`, the lowest
of the three fitted models, because R² also counts how far below the catch they sit. This
is the left card of the diagram above, in real predictions. Predicting the average scores
an R² of `r f3(r2_of("Predicting the average", "R²"))`, about zero, as R² is defined
against it.

### MAE would scale the forest's predictions down

Multiplying every prediction of the random forest by the same number shows where each
measure wants the predictions to be. The measure is lowest at the scaling it prefers.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: scaling
forest_only <- filter(predictions, model == "Random forest")

curves <- tibble(scaling = seq(0.5, 1.5, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(RMSE = map_dbl(scaling, \(k) rmse_vec(forest_only$caught,
                                                k * forest_only$predicted)),
         MAE = map_dbl(scaling, \(k) mae_vec(forest_only$caught,
                                              k * forest_only$predicted)),
         `Poisson deviance` = map_dbl(scaling, \(k) poisson_deviance(
           forest_only$caught, k * forest_only$predicted))) |>
  pivot_longer(-scaling, names_to = "measure") |>
  mutate(measure = fct_inorder(measure))

# the scaling at which each measure is lowest
lowest <- slice_min(curves, value, by = measure)
lowest |> mutate(value = round(value, 2))
```

## Python

```{python}
forest_only = predictions[predictions["model"] == "Random forest"]
scalings = np.round(np.arange(0.5, 1.505, 0.01), 2)

measures = {"RMSE": root_mean_squared_error, "MAE": mean_absolute_error,
            "Poisson deviance": mean_poisson_deviance}
curves = pd.DataFrame([
    {"scaling": k, "measure": name,
     "value": measure(forest_only["caught"], k * forest_only["predicted"])}
    for name, measure in measures.items() for k in scalings])

# the scaling at which each measure is lowest
lowest = curves.loc[curves.groupby("measure", sort=False)["value"].idxmin()]
lowest.reset_index(drop=True).round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: scaling-numbers
#| include: false
best_scaling <- function(name) lowest$scaling[lowest$measure == name]
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-scaling
#| fig-cap: !expr glue::glue("The three measures for the random forest's predictions, each multiplied by the same number, and each drawn relative to its own lowest value. The RMSE and the Poisson deviance are lowest close to 1, where the forest already is; MAE is lowest where every prediction is multiplied by {f2(best_scaling('MAE'))}.")
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Three panels side by side, for RMSE, MAE and Poisson deviance, each with the number every prediction is multiplied by along the bottom, from 0.5 to 1.5, and the measure relative to its lowest value up the side. Each is a U-shaped curve with a point at its lowest value. The RMSE is lowest at {f2(best_scaling('RMSE'))}, the Poisson deviance at {f2(best_scaling('Poisson deviance'))}, and MAE at {f2(best_scaling('MAE'))}, further left than the other two.")
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
curves <- mutate(curves, relative = value / min(value), .by = measure)
at_lowest <- semi_join(curves, lowest, by = c("measure", "scaling"))

ggplot(curves, aes(scaling, relative, colour = measure)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = at_lowest, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = at_lowest,
            aes(y = Inf, label = sprintf("lowest at %.2f", scaling)),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_ml() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "Every prediction multiplied by",
       y = "Measure relative\nto its lowest") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

:::

The RMSE is lowest at `r f2(best_scaling("RMSE"))` and the Poisson deviance at
`r f2(best_scaling("Poisson deviance"))`: both would leave the forest's predictions
close to where they are. MAE is lowest at `r f2(best_scaling("MAE"))`, close to the
`r f2(score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` at which the forest on log counts
predicts the catch. MAE preferred that forest because it predicts low, not because it
follows the catch better.

## A total needs a measure aimed at the average

When predictions are summed into a total, such as a stock estimate, a map of abundance or
a bycatch figure, score them with a measure aimed at the average: the RMSE, or the
Poisson deviance, which compares each miss with the count predicted. Report R² as
`rsq_trad()` or `r2_score()`, not the squared correlation, and check the predicted total
against the observed one. MAE suits a question about the typical station, where totals do
not matter. [Choosing measures that match the objective](choosing-a-metric.qmd) takes
this further.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- **RMSE, MAE, the Poisson deviance and R²** weigh misses differently. The RMSE and the
  Poisson deviance are lowest at the average of what could be observed, MAE at the median.
- On these skewed counts the RMSE picked the `r str_to_lower(best_on("RMSE"))` and MAE the
  `r str_to_lower(best_on("MAE"))`, which predicts only
  `r pct(score_of(log_forest, "predicted / caught"))` of the animals caught.
- The **squared correlation**, yardstick's `rsq()`, cannot see predictions that are too
  low across the board. The textbook **R²**, `rsq_trad()` or `r2_score()`, can: it put the
  forest on log counts last of the fitted models.
- MAE would scale the random forest's predictions down to `r f2(best_scaling("MAE"))` of
  their size; the RMSE and the Poisson deviance would leave them close to where they are.
- MAPE is undefined for a count of zero and favours low predictions. Do not use it for
  counts.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Add MAPE (`mape_vec()`) to the scaling curves, scored on the stations that caught
   something. Predict first: is it lowest above or below MAE's scaling?
2. Multiply the forest on log counts' predictions by one number, chosen so that their
   total matches the catch of the fitted stations in each fold. How much do its RMSE, MAE
   and R² change?
